analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial regulator's funding from the Federal Reserve to annual congressional appropriations.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced in May 2015 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, it saw no further action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is funded. Under current law, the bureau draws its budget as a set share from the Federal Reserve, keeping it out of the yearly congressional budget fights. The bill would replace that with annual appropriations, meaning Congress could cut, cap, or threaten the bureau's budget from year to year. The bureau polices banks, credit card companies, debt collectors, and other financial firms on behalf of consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Financial companies regulated by the CFPB — banks, credit card issuers, debt collectors, and other lenders — would benefit, because annual appropriations would let Congress reduce or politicize the bureau's budget and limit its enforcement work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the CFPB's automatic funding stream from the Federal Reserve and replaces it with money Congress must approve each year [S2] [S3].
Under current law, transfers from the Federal Reserve let the CFPB operate entirely outside the annual congressional appropriations process [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost: a CFPB whose budget must be renewed annually is easier for lawmakers to defund or hold hostage, which weakens the agency that refunds wronged customers and enforces rules against abusive lending.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of the current structure argue that the Federal Reserve funding stream exists precisely so the consumer watchdog cannot be defunded by the financial interests it regulates, and that annual appropriations would expose the bureau to exactly that pressure [S2].

Supporters of the bill contend it is a fairness fix, since most other financial regulators already operate on congressional appropriations and the CFPB's self-funding removes a routine check on its budget; the bill's own framing is that the bureau should be accountable to Congress [S2] [S3].
Either funding model has a cost: appropriations add political leverage over enforcement, while the current structure reduces Congress's ordinary oversight of a spending agency's budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades oversight for vulnerability. Moving the CFPB to appropriations would give Congress a more normal grip on its budget, but it would also hand the financial industry a recurring opportunity to shrink the regulator through the annual budget process. Since the industries the bureau polices are among the most active lobbying forces in Washington, the practical effect leans heavily toward weakening consumer enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator David Perdue introduced the bill on May 19, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action are listed before the Congress ended [S5].
Seventeen senators, all Republicans, cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The CFPB kept its independent Federal Reserve funding stream, so banks, debt collectors, and other regulated firms did not get the appropriations lever they sought, and the agency's consumer enforcement continued uninterrupted.

for.name: David Perdue
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee.

for.name: 17 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to move the CFPB to annual appropriations.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and the Banking Committee never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, debt collectors, and other firms regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: Annual appropriations would let Congress pressure or cut the budget of the agency that enforces consumer financial rules against these firms, easing enforcement and restitution. Consumers would lose the counterweight.
The bill strips the bureau's independent funding and makes its budget hostage to annual approval, which would likely reduce the enforcement and refund work it does for consumers.
The bill transfers spending power over the bureau from the Federal Reserve to the congressional appropriations process, a genuine structural gain for congressional oversight.
